UC00219 - Thermal Hotspot vs Tree Canopy Overlay
Authored by: Thien Khang Nguyen
Duration: 90 mins
Level: Intermediate
Pre-requisite Skills: Python, Data Cleaning, Data Visualisation, Geospatial Analysis, Raster/Vector Data Handling, Spatial Overlay, Feature Interpretation

Scenario

Melbourne does not experience heat evenly. Some blocks and streets become much hotter than nearby areas, especially where vegetation is limited.

This project asks a practical planning question: which grid cells combine high relative thermal intensity with very low tree canopy cover, and should therefore be treated as greening priority zones?

The analysis is designed for decision support rather than pure mapping. Outputs are intended to help explain where intervention might matter most and why those locations are defensible priorities.

Introduction

Urban heat vulnerability is strongly influenced by land cover. Built surfaces store and re-radiate heat, while tree canopy provides shading and cooling benefits. To make this relationship measurable, the notebook combines a thermal raster (2012) and canopy polygons (2021) into a shared analysis grid.

Research questions

  1. Where are the highest relative thermal-intensity cells in the study area?
  2. Which of those hot cells also have low canopy cover?
  3. Do data-driven clusters confirm the same hotspot patterns identified by the rule-based method?

Method choices and justification

  • 250 m grid: balances local spatial detail with stable per-cell summary statistics.
  • Top-25% thermal ranking: avoids instability when many cells share similar maximum thermal values.
  • Low canopy threshold (5%): isolates cells with clearly limited vegetation rather than moderate canopy levels.
  • KMeans + silhouette comparison: provides a transparent baseline unsupervised model and objective k selection.

Interpretation scope Because thermal and canopy layers come from different years, results are interpreted as exploratory spatial evidence (relative priority), not causal proof.

2. Loading the Tree Canopy Dataset¶

This code reads tree canopy data from City of Melbourne public API v2.1 endpoints. Using public sources keeps the workflow reproducible and avoids exposing credentials. The loaded canopy polygons are the vector layer used later in grid overlay analysis.

In [2]:
# Load tree canopy data from Melbourne Open Data API v2.1 (GeoJSON export).
canopy_api_url = (
    "https://data.melbourne.vic.gov.au/api/explore/v2.1/catalog/datasets/"
    "tree-canopies-2021-urban-forest/exports/geojson?limit=-1"
)

response = requests.get(canopy_api_url, timeout=180)
response.raise_for_status()
canopy_geojson = response.json()

if "features" not in canopy_geojson or not canopy_geojson["features"]:
    raise ValueError("Canopy API returned no features.")

canopy_gdf = gpd.GeoDataFrame.from_features(canopy_geojson["features"])
if canopy_gdf.crs is None:
    canopy_gdf = canopy_gdf.set_crs(epsg=4326)

print("Tree canopy dataset loaded successfully from API 2.1.")
print("API URL:", canopy_api_url)

8. Loading the Thermal Image Dataset¶

This step loads the thermal image as raster data from public City of Melbourne sources. Raster pixels are handled differently from vector polygons, so the processing path is separate. The raster layer provides the thermal values later summarised per grid cell.

In [12]:
# Load thermal image data from Melbourne Open Data API v2.1 attachments.
thermal_meta_url = (
    "https://data.melbourne.vic.gov.au/api/explore/v2.1/catalog/datasets/"
    "thermal-image-2012"
)

meta_response = requests.get(thermal_meta_url, timeout=120)
meta_response.raise_for_status()
thermal_meta = meta_response.json()

attachments = thermal_meta.get("attachments", [])
if not attachments:
    raise ValueError("Thermal dataset API returned no attachments.")

preferred_attachment_ids = ("geotiff_1_zip", "clipped_thermal_zip", "geotiff_2_zip")
selected_attachment = None
for attachment_id in preferred_attachment_ids:
    selected_attachment = next(
        (item for item in attachments if item.get("id") == attachment_id),
        None,
    )
    if selected_attachment is not None:
        break

if selected_attachment is None:
    selected_attachment = attachments[0]

thermal_zip_url = selected_attachment.get("url")
if not thermal_zip_url:
    raise ValueError("Selected thermal attachment has no download URL.")

thermal_cache_dir = Path(tempfile.gettempdir()) / "project60_thermal"
thermal_cache_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

zip_id = selected_attachment.get("id", "thermal_attachment")
zip_path = thermal_cache_dir / f"{zip_id}.zip"
extract_dir = thermal_cache_dir / zip_id
extract_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

if not zip_path.exists():
    zip_response = requests.get(thermal_zip_url, timeout=180)
    zip_response.raise_for_status()
    zip_path.write_bytes(zip_response.content)

with zipfile.ZipFile(zip_path, "r") as zf:
    zf.extractall(extract_dir)

tif_candidates = list(extract_dir.rglob("*.tif")) + list(extract_dir.rglob("*.tiff"))
if not tif_candidates:
    raise FileNotFoundError("No GeoTIFF file found in downloaded thermal attachment.")

thermal_tif_path = tif_candidates[0]
thermal_src = rasterio.open(thermal_tif_path)

print("Thermal image dataset loaded successfully from API 2.1.")
print("Metadata URL:", thermal_meta_url)
print("Attachment URL:", thermal_zip_url)
print("GeoTIFF path:", thermal_tif_path)

17. Creating an Analysis Grid¶

Here the notebook creates a 250 m grid across the study area. The grid gives canopy and thermal data the same spatial unit, so both can be compared cell by cell. This common structure supports stable summaries and practical hotspot prioritisation.

In [26]:
# Create a grid based on the thermal image bounds.
minx, miny, maxx, maxy = thermal_src.bounds

cell_size = 250  # in metres

grid_cells = []
x = minx
while x < maxx:
    y = miny
    while y < maxy:
        grid_cells.append(box(x, y, x + cell_size, y + cell_size))
        y += cell_size
    x += cell_size

grid_gdf = gpd.GeoDataFrame({"geometry": grid_cells}, crs=thermal_src.crs)

print("Grid created successfully.")
print("Number of grid cells:", len(grid_gdf))

Grid created successfully.

21. Summarising Canopy Area by Grid Cell¶

This section aggregates intersected canopy fragments into one canopy-area value per grid cell. The summary creates a clean cell-level vegetation indicator used in hotspot and clustering workflows.

22. Calculating Canopy Cover Percentage¶

This code converts intersected canopy area into a canopy percentage for each grid cell. A percentage is needed so vegetation levels are directly comparable across cells. The canopy_cover_pct field is then used in hotspot rules and clustering features.

In [38]:
# Merge the canopy totals back into the grid.
grid_gdf = grid_gdf.merge(canopy_by_grid, on="grid_id", how="left")

# Fill missing canopy values with 0.
grid_gdf["intersection_area_m2"] = grid_gdf["intersection_area_m2"].fillna(0)

# Calculate canopy cover percentage.
grid_gdf["canopy_cover_pct"] = (grid_gdf["intersection_area_m2"] / grid_gdf["grid_area_m2"]) * 100

23. Calculating Thermal Intensity for Each Grid Cell¶

This step calculates mean thermal intensity from raster pixels within each grid cell. Cell-level aggregation is needed so thermal values match the same unit used for canopy coverage. The resulting mean_thermal field is used in both hotspot selection and cluster modelling.

In [40]:
# Calculate one thermal value for each grid cell.
thermal_means = []
no_usable_thermal_cells = 0

for geom in grid_gdf.geometry:
    try:
        # Read band 1 only so the metric is consistent across all cells.
        out_image, _ = mask(thermal_src, [geom], crop=True)
        data = out_image[0].astype(float)

        # Treat only background value (0) as missing.
        data[data <= 0] = np.nan

        if np.isnan(data).all():
            thermal_means.append(np.nan)
            no_usable_thermal_cells += 1
        else:
            thermal_means.append(np.nanmean(data))
    except Exception:
        thermal_means.append(np.nan)
        no_usable_thermal_cells += 1

grid_gdf["mean_thermal"] = thermal_means

print(grid_gdf["mean_thermal"].head())
print("Cells with no usable thermal pixels:", no_usable_thermal_cells)

25. Identifying High Thermal and Low Canopy Cells¶

This section applies a transparent rule that combines high relative thermal intensity with low canopy cover. The rule-based approach makes prioritisation easy to explain, check, and reproduce. It directly answers the UC00219 question by flagging candidate hotspot cells.

In [44]:
# Define thresholds for hotspot rules.
thermal_max = grid_gdf["mean_thermal"].max()
quantile_candidates = [0.75, 0.70, 0.65, 0.60, 0.55, 0.50, 0.45, 0.40]
selected_quantile = None
thermal_threshold = np.nan

for q in quantile_candidates:
    candidate_threshold = grid_gdf["mean_thermal"].quantile(q)
    if candidate_threshold < thermal_max:
        thermal_threshold = candidate_threshold
        selected_quantile = q
        break

if selected_quantile is None:
    selected_quantile = 0.25
    thermal_threshold = grid_gdf["mean_thermal"].quantile(selected_quantile)

canopy_threshold = 5.0

print("Thermal max:", thermal_max)
print("Chosen thermal quantile:", selected_quantile)
print("Chosen thermal threshold:", thermal_threshold)
print("Canopy threshold:", canopy_threshold)
print("Note: Many cells share the max value, so the next step uses a top-25% ranking rule for high thermal selection.")

Canopy threshold: 5.0

# Create classification columns.
valid_thermal = grid_gdf[["mean_thermal", "canopy_cover_pct"]].dropna(subset=["mean_thermal"]).sort_values(
    ["mean_thermal", "canopy_cover_pct"],
    ascending=[False, True]
)
top_thermal_count = int(np.ceil(len(valid_thermal) * 0.25))
high_thermal_index = valid_thermal.index[:top_thermal_count]

grid_gdf["high_thermal"] = False
grid_gdf.loc[high_thermal_index, "high_thermal"] = True
grid_gdf["low_canopy"] = grid_gdf["canopy_cover_pct"] < canopy_threshold

# Final priority cells.
grid_gdf["priority_cell"] = grid_gdf["high_thermal"] & grid_gdf["low_canopy"]

print("Cells in top 25% thermal group:", top_thermal_count)

29. Hotspot Interpretation¶

This section explains the rule logic in plain language so the method can be clearly communicated. It links the code-based hotspot criteria to the UC00219 workflow before moving into clustering analysis.

The hotspot method combines two explicit rules:

  1. Select the top 25% of cells by mean_thermal (with canopy as tie-breaker when needed).
  2. Keep only cells with canopy_cover_pct < 5.

This design is intentionally transparent and presentation-friendly: each rule has a direct planning meaning, and each can be stress-tested with sensitivity analysis.

Interpretation should remain relative. The thermal layer captures image intensity patterns, so the result is a priority map of hotter-than-average, low-canopy cells, not absolute temperature in degrees Celsius.

The clustering stage is used as a complementary validation lens: if high-priority cells also concentrate in the same high-thermal/low-canopy clusters, confidence in the spatial signal increases.

30. Building a Hotspot Clustering Model¶

This stage builds a baseline clustering model using canopy and thermal features. Clustering is used as a complementary pattern-detection method, not a replacement for the hotspot rule. Together, the two methods provide both transparent logic and data-driven structure checks.

This section builds an unsupervised clustering model to group grid cells based on their thermal intensity and tree canopy cover.

The aim is to identify whether the study area naturally separates into different hotspot-related patterns, such as high thermal intensity with low canopy cover, or lower thermal intensity with higher canopy presence.

In [50]:
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score

31. Preparing Features for Clustering¶

This section selects the two main indicators, mean_thermal and canopy_cover_pct, as clustering features. The values are standardised so both variables contribute fairly to the KMeans model instead of one feature dominating because of scale differences.

In [51]:
# Select features for clustering.
if "grid_gdf" not in globals():
    raise RuntimeError(
        "grid_gdf is not available. Please run the notebook from the beginning (Run All) before Section 31."
    )

required_cols = {"mean_thermal", "canopy_cover_pct"}
missing_cols = required_cols - set(grid_gdf.columns)
if missing_cols:
    raise RuntimeError(
        f"Missing columns for clustering: {sorted(missing_cols)}. Please run earlier sections first."
    )

clustering_data = grid_gdf[["mean_thermal", "canopy_cover_pct"]].copy()

# Fill missing values with median so KMeans can run safely.
missing_before = clustering_data.isna().sum()
clustering_data["mean_thermal"] = clustering_data["mean_thermal"].fillna(clustering_data["mean_thermal"].median())
clustering_data["canopy_cover_pct"] = clustering_data["canopy_cover_pct"].fillna(clustering_data["canopy_cover_pct"].median())
missing_after = clustering_data.isna().sum()

print("Missing values before fill:")
print(missing_before)
print("Missing values after fill:")
print(missing_after)
print(clustering_data.head())

32. Training the KMeans Model¶

This section trains KMeans models using several possible cluster counts. Comparing silhouette score and inertia helps choose a cluster count that gives useful grouping without making the model unnecessarily complex.

In [53]:
# Compare candidate k values before final model selection.
k_candidates = [3, 4, 5, 6]
comparison_rows = []

for k in k_candidates:
    candidate_model = KMeans(n_clusters=k, random_state=42, n_init=10)
    candidate_labels = candidate_model.fit_predict(X_scaled)
    comparison_rows.append({
        "k": k,
        "inertia": candidate_model.inertia_,
        "silhouette_score": silhouette_score(X_scaled, candidate_labels)
    })

kmeans_comparison = pd.DataFrame(comparison_rows).sort_values("k").reset_index(drop=True)
print("k comparison table:")
print(kmeans_comparison)

best_k = int(kmeans_comparison.loc[kmeans_comparison["silhouette_score"].idxmax(), "k"])
print("Selected k based on silhouette score:", best_k)

# Train final KMeans model using justified k.
kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=best_k, random_state=42, n_init=10)
grid_gdf["cluster"] = kmeans.fit_predict(X_scaled)

print(grid_gdf["cluster"].value_counts().sort_index())

35. Sensitivity Analysis for Hotspot Rules¶

This code tests nearby thermal-share and canopy thresholds around the baseline settings. The goal is to check whether hotspot results depend too heavily on one specific threshold choice. That sensitivity check strengthens confidence in the prioritisation workflow.

In [58]:
# Sensitivity check for rule-based hotspot settings.
required_cols = {"mean_thermal", "canopy_cover_pct"}
missing_cols = required_cols - set(grid_gdf.columns)
if missing_cols:
    raise RuntimeError(
        f"Missing columns for sensitivity analysis: {sorted(missing_cols)}. Run earlier hotspot sections first."
    )

valid_base = grid_gdf[["mean_thermal", "canopy_cover_pct"]].dropna(subset=["mean_thermal"]).sort_values(
    ["mean_thermal", "canopy_cover_pct"],
    ascending=[False, True]
)

thermal_shares = [0.20, 0.25, 0.30]
canopy_thresholds = [3.0, 5.0, 10.0]
sensitivity_rows = []

for thermal_share in thermal_shares:
    top_n = int(np.ceil(len(valid_base) * thermal_share))
    high_thermal_idx = valid_base.index[:top_n]

    for canopy_limit in canopy_thresholds:
        priority_flag = grid_gdf.index.isin(high_thermal_idx) & (grid_gdf["canopy_cover_pct"] < canopy_limit)
        priority_subset = grid_gdf.loc[priority_flag, ["mean_thermal", "canopy_cover_pct"]]

        sensitivity_rows.append({
            "thermal_top_share": thermal_share,
            "canopy_threshold_pct": canopy_limit,
            "priority_cells": int(priority_flag.sum()),
            "priority_pct_of_grid": float(priority_flag.mean() * 100),
            "priority_mean_thermal": float(priority_subset["mean_thermal"].mean()) if len(priority_subset) else np.nan,
            "priority_mean_canopy": float(priority_subset["canopy_cover_pct"].mean()) if len(priority_subset) else np.nan,
        })

sensitivity_df = pd.DataFrame(sensitivity_rows)
print("Hotspot sensitivity summary:")
print(sensitivity_df.to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda x: f"{x:0.3f}"))

selected_setup = sensitivity_df[
    (sensitivity_df["thermal_top_share"] == 0.25)
    & (sensitivity_df["canopy_threshold_pct"] == 5.0)
]

if not selected_setup.empty:
    row = selected_setup.iloc[0]
    print("\nSelected setup check (top 25%, canopy < 5%):")
    print(
        f"priority_cells={int(row['priority_cells'])}, "
        f"priority_pct_of_grid={row['priority_pct_of_grid']:.2f}, "
        f"priority_mean_thermal={row['priority_mean_thermal']:.3f}, "
        f"priority_mean_canopy={row['priority_mean_canopy']:.3f}"
    )

36. Deeper Comparative Analysis¶

This section compares summary statistics between priority and non-priority cells. The comparison quantifies how different the two groups are, rather than relying only on maps. It also links these differences to cluster outputs for a cross-method check.

37. Presentation-Ready Takeaways¶

  • Main signal: hotspot cells consistently combine higher relative thermal intensity with very low canopy cover.
  • Why this is defensible: rules are explicit, reproducible, and checked with sensitivity tests.
  • Why clustering was added: it provides an independent pattern check beyond rule-based thresholds.
  • Planning implication: prioritize greening/shade interventions in cells repeatedly flagged by both rule-based and cluster-based views.
  • Caveat to state clearly: outputs represent exploratory spatial priority, not direct causal temperature effects, due to dataset year mismatch.

38. Improve Model: Candidate Search and Stability¶

This section runs a candidate search across scaler type, cluster count, and random seed settings. It checks whether different standardisation and initialisation choices produce stable quality metrics. The purpose is to validate a reasonable configuration, not to claim major model improvement.

In [60]:
from sklearn.preprocessing import RobustScaler
from sklearn.metrics import davies_bouldin_score, calinski_harabasz_score, adjusted_rand_score

required_cols = {"mean_thermal", "canopy_cover_pct", "priority_cell"}
missing_cols = required_cols - set(grid_gdf.columns)
if missing_cols:
    raise RuntimeError(
        f"Missing columns for improve-model stage: {sorted(missing_cols)}. Run sections 25-37 first."
    )

# Keep baseline labels from earlier section for later comparison.
if "cluster" in grid_gdf.columns:
    grid_gdf["cluster_baseline"] = grid_gdf["cluster"].astype(int)

feature_df = grid_gdf[["mean_thermal", "canopy_cover_pct"]].copy()
feature_df["mean_thermal"] = feature_df["mean_thermal"].fillna(feature_df["mean_thermal"].median())
feature_df["canopy_cover_pct"] = feature_df["canopy_cover_pct"].fillna(feature_df["canopy_cover_pct"].median())

scalers = {
    "standard": StandardScaler(),
    "robust": RobustScaler()
}

k_candidates = [2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
seed_candidates = [7, 21, 42, 84, 126]
comparison_rows = []

for scaler_name, scaler in scalers.items():
    X_candidate = scaler.fit_transform(feature_df)

    for k in k_candidates:
        labels_runs = []
        sil_scores = []
        db_scores = []
        ch_scores = []
        inertias = []

        for seed in seed_candidates:
            model = KMeans(n_clusters=k, random_state=seed, n_init=20)
            labels = model.fit_predict(X_candidate)
            labels_runs.append(labels)
            sil_scores.append(silhouette_score(X_candidate, labels))
            db_scores.append(davies_bouldin_score(X_candidate, labels))
            ch_scores.append(calinski_harabasz_score(X_candidate, labels))
            inertias.append(model.inertia_)

        pairwise_ari = []
        for i in range(len(labels_runs)):
            for j in range(i + 1, len(labels_runs)):
                pairwise_ari.append(adjusted_rand_score(labels_runs[i], labels_runs[j]))

        comparison_rows.append({
            "scaler": scaler_name,
            "k": k,
            "silhouette_mean": float(np.mean(sil_scores)),
            "silhouette_std": float(np.std(sil_scores)),
            "db_mean": float(np.mean(db_scores)),
            "ch_mean": float(np.mean(ch_scores)),
            "inertia_mean": float(np.mean(inertias)),
            "stability_ari_mean": float(np.mean(pairwise_ari)),
        })

improve_search_df = pd.DataFrame(comparison_rows)
improve_search_df = improve_search_df.sort_values(
    ["silhouette_mean", "stability_ari_mean", "db_mean"],
    ascending=[False, False, True]
).reset_index(drop=True)

print("Top improve-model candidates:")
print(improve_search_df.head(8).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda x: f"{x:0.4f}"))

This section uses the best candidate configuration from the search step to create the selected cluster labels. It keeps the final clustering setup reproducible and based on validation results rather than a random manual choice.

The candidate search tested multiple scalers, cluster counts, and random seeds to validate the clustering setup.

42. Final Interpretation¶

The identified hotspot cells represent relative priority areas where thermal intensity is high and tree canopy coverage is very low.

Combining these two indicators is useful because it links a heat-exposure signal (mean_thermal) with a modifiable urban factor (canopy_cover_pct).

Sensitivity analysis shows whether hotspot outputs stay broadly consistent under nearby threshold choices, reducing dependence on one exact rule setting.

The priority vs non-priority comparison quantifies the gap in canopy and thermal profiles, providing stronger evidence than map visuals alone.

Clustering adds a pattern-based view beyond the rule-based method by grouping cells into canopy-thermal profiles, supporting communication of different intervention contexts.

Together, the rule-based and clustering outputs support practical greening/planning discussions about where shade and canopy investment may be most beneficial.

43. Limitations and Future Work¶

  • Thermal raster values appear to be relative intensity values (0-255 style range), not direct Celsius measurements.
  • Many cells can reach the maximum value (e.g., 255), so hotspots should be interpreted as relative priority indicators, not exact temperature readings.
  • Thermal and canopy datasets come from different years, so outputs are exploratory and should not be interpreted as causal proof of same-time canopy-temperature effects.
  • This workflow is not a real-time heat monitoring system.

Future work

  • Include newer thermal imagery and temporal comparison.
  • Add land-use, built-form, and population exposure variables.
  • Add ground validation against in-situ observations where available.
  • Explore more advanced spatial/statistical modelling while preserving interpretability.

44. Lightweight Threshold Tuning¶

This step runs a lightweight threshold-tuning check around the main hotspot settings. It tests whether small parameter changes alter priority counts or ranking behaviour too strongly. The tuning output supports robustness reporting before final handover.

In [65]:
# Lightweight threshold tuning around the baseline rule.
required_cols = {"mean_thermal", "canopy_cover_pct"}
missing_cols = required_cols - set(grid_gdf.columns)
if missing_cols:
    raise RuntimeError(f"Missing columns for threshold tuning: {sorted(missing_cols)}")

valid_rank = grid_gdf[["mean_thermal", "canopy_cover_pct"]].dropna(subset=["mean_thermal"]).sort_values(
    ["mean_thermal", "canopy_cover_pct"],
    ascending=[False, True]
)

thermal_top_share_list = [0.20, 0.25, 0.30]
canopy_threshold_list = [0.03, 0.05, 0.10]  # fractions corresponding to 3%, 5%, 10%
threshold_rows = []

for thermal_top_share in thermal_top_share_list:
    top_n = int(np.ceil(len(valid_rank) * thermal_top_share))
    high_idx = valid_rank.index[:top_n]

    for canopy_threshold in canopy_threshold_list:
        canopy_threshold_pct = canopy_threshold * 100
        is_priority = grid_gdf.index.isin(high_idx) & (grid_gdf["canopy_cover_pct"] < canopy_threshold_pct)
        subset = grid_gdf.loc[is_priority, ["mean_thermal", "canopy_cover_pct"]]

        threshold_rows.append({
            "thermal_top_share": thermal_top_share,
            "canopy_threshold": canopy_threshold,
            "priority_cell_count": int(is_priority.sum()),
            "priority_cell_percent": float(is_priority.mean() * 100),
            "priority_mean_thermal": float(subset["mean_thermal"].mean()) if len(subset) else np.nan,
            "priority_mean_canopy": float(subset["canopy_cover_pct"].mean()) if len(subset) else np.nan,
        })

threshold_tuning_df = pd.DataFrame(threshold_rows).sort_values(["thermal_top_share", "canopy_threshold"]).reset_index(drop=True)
hotspot_sensitivity_summary_df = threshold_tuning_df.copy()

print("Lightweight threshold tuning summary:")
print(threshold_tuning_df.to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda x: f"{x:0.3f}"))

45. Normalised Hotspot Score v2¶

This section creates a simple score by combining normalised thermal intensity with low canopy cover. The score is used only as an exploratory ranking aid, not as a validated scientific risk index.

In [66]:
# Min-max normalised hotspot score (v2).
score_input = grid_gdf[["mean_thermal", "canopy_cover_pct"]].copy()
score_input["mean_thermal"] = score_input["mean_thermal"].fillna(score_input["mean_thermal"].median())
score_input["canopy_cover_pct"] = score_input["canopy_cover_pct"].fillna(score_input["canopy_cover_pct"].median())

def minmax_norm(series):
    s_min = float(series.min())
    s_max = float(series.max())
    if np.isclose(s_max, s_min):
        return pd.Series(0.5, index=series.index)
    return (series - s_min) / (s_max - s_min)

grid_gdf["thermal_norm"] = minmax_norm(score_input["mean_thermal"])
grid_gdf["canopy_norm"] = minmax_norm(score_input["canopy_cover_pct"])
grid_gdf["low_canopy_norm"] = 1 - grid_gdf["canopy_norm"]
grid_gdf["hotspot_score_v2"] = (0.6 * grid_gdf["thermal_norm"]) + (0.4 * grid_gdf["low_canopy_norm"])

top_hotspot_score_v2_df = grid_gdf.sort_values("hotspot_score_v2", ascending=False)[
    [c for c in ["grid_id", "mean_thermal", "canopy_cover_pct", "hotspot_score_v2", "priority_cell", "cluster"] if c in grid_gdf.columns]
].head(10)

print("Top cells by hotspot_score_v2:")
print(top_hotspot_score_v2_df)

45.1 Presentation-Friendly Cluster Labels¶

This section assigns readable labels to clusters for communication. The labels make outputs easier for non-technical reviewers to follow during presentation and review. Numeric cluster IDs remain the underlying model outputs used in analysis.

In [67]:
# Create communication labels from cluster profiles.
cluster_col = "cluster_improved" if "cluster_improved" in grid_gdf.columns else "cluster"
if cluster_col not in grid_gdf.columns:
    raise RuntimeError("No cluster column found. Run clustering sections first.")

cluster_profile_summary_df = grid_gdf.groupby(cluster_col).agg(
    cell_count=("grid_id", "count") if "grid_id" in grid_gdf.columns else ("mean_thermal", "count"),
    mean_canopy_cover_pct=("canopy_cover_pct", "mean"),
    mean_thermal=("mean_thermal", "mean"),
    priority_cell_rate_pct=("priority_cell", lambda s: float(s.mean() * 100)),
).reset_index().rename(columns={cluster_col: "cluster_id"})

if "hotspot_score_v2" in grid_gdf.columns:
    score_means = grid_gdf.groupby(cluster_col)["hotspot_score_v2"].mean().reset_index(drop=True)
    cluster_profile_summary_df["mean_hotspot_score_v2"] = score_means
else:
    cluster_profile_summary_df["mean_hotspot_score_v2"] = np.nan

thermal_cut = cluster_profile_summary_df["mean_thermal"].median()
canopy_cut = cluster_profile_summary_df["mean_canopy_cover_pct"].median()

cluster_label_map = {}
for _, row in cluster_profile_summary_df.iterrows():
    cid = int(row["cluster_id"])
    heat_text = "High thermal" if row["mean_thermal"] >= thermal_cut else "Lower thermal"
    canopy_text = "Low canopy" if row["mean_canopy_cover_pct"] <= canopy_cut else "Higher canopy"
    cluster_label_map[cid] = f"{heat_text} / {canopy_text} (C{cid})"

grid_gdf["cluster_label"] = grid_gdf[cluster_col].astype(int).map(cluster_label_map)

cluster_profile_summary_df["cluster_label"] = cluster_profile_summary_df["cluster_id"].astype(int).map(cluster_label_map)
cluster_profile_summary_df = cluster_profile_summary_df[[
    "cluster_id", "cluster_label", "cell_count", "mean_canopy_cover_pct",
    "mean_thermal", "mean_hotspot_score_v2", "priority_cell_rate_pct"
]]

print("Cluster profile summary with communication labels:")
print(cluster_profile_summary_df.round(3))

    hotspot_sensitivity_export_df = hotspot_sensitivity_summary_df.copy()
elif "sensitivity_df" in globals():
    hotspot_sensitivity_export_df = sensitivity_df.copy()
else:
    hotspot_sensitivity_export_df = pd.DataFrame()
    export_warnings.append("No sensitivity summary DataFrame found; exported empty hotspot_sensitivity_summary.csv")
hotspot_sensitivity_export_df.to_csv(output_dir / "hotspot_sensitivity_summary.csv", index=False)

# 3) cluster_profile_summary.csv
if "cluster_profile_summary_df" in globals():
    cluster_profile_export_df = cluster_profile_summary_df.copy()
else:
    cluster_profile_export_df = pd.DataFrame()
    export_warnings.append("No cluster profile summary found; exported empty cluster_profile_summary.csv")
cluster_profile_export_df.to_csv(output_dir / "cluster_profile_summary.csv", index=False)

# 4) model_comparison_summary.csv
if "comparison_table" in globals():
    model_comparison_summary_df = comparison_table.copy()
else:
    model_comparison_summary_df = pd.DataFrame()
    export_warnings.append("No model comparison table found; exported empty model_comparison_summary.csv")

selected_config_text = f"scaler={globals().get('selected_scaler_name', 'unknown')}, k={globals().get('selected_k', 'unknown')}, random_state=42"
if not model_comparison_summary_df.empty:
    model_comparison_summary_df["selected_config"] = selected_config_text
model_comparison_summary_df.to_csv(output_dir / "model_comparison_summary.csv", index=False)

# 5) final_hotspot_summary.txt
total_cells_out = int(len(grid_gdf))
priority_cells_out = int(grid_gdf["priority_cell"].sum())
priority_pct_out = float((priority_cells_out / total_cells_out) * 100) if total_cells_out else 0.0
priority_mean_thermal_out = float(grid_gdf.loc[grid_gdf["priority_cell"], "mean_thermal"].mean())
priority_mean_canopy_out = float(grid_gdf.loc[grid_gdf["priority_cell"], "canopy_cover_pct"].mean())

baseline_row = None
selected_row = None
if "model_comparison_summary_df" in globals() and not model_comparison_summary_df.empty and "model_version" in model_comparison_summary_df.columns:
    baseline_match = model_comparison_summary_df[model_comparison_summary_df["model_version"] == "baseline"]
    improved_match = model_comparison_summary_df[model_comparison_summary_df["model_version"] == "improved"]
    if len(baseline_match):
        baseline_row = baseline_match.iloc[0].to_dict()
    if len(improved_match):
        selected_row = improved_match.iloc[0].to_dict()

summary_lines = [
    "UC00219 Final Hotspot Summary",
    "================================",
    f"Total grid cells: {total_cells_out}",
    f"Priority cells: {priority_cells_out}",
    f"Priority cell percentage: {priority_pct_out:.2f}%",
    f"Mean thermal intensity (priority cells): {priority_mean_thermal_out:.3f}",
    f"Mean canopy cover % (priority cells): {priority_mean_canopy_out:.3f}",
    f"Selected clustering configuration: {selected_config_text}",
]

if baseline_row is not None and selected_row is not None:
    summary_lines.extend([
        "",
        "Baseline vs selected model summary:",
        f"- Baseline silhouette: {baseline_row.get('silhouette', float('nan')):.4f}",
        f"- Selected silhouette: {selected_row.get('silhouette', float('nan')):.4f}",
        f"- Baseline Davies-Bouldin: {baseline_row.get('davies_bouldin', float('nan')):.4f}",
        f"- Selected Davies-Bouldin: {selected_row.get('davies_bouldin', float('nan')):.4f}",
        "- Note: candidate search is used as validation/stability evidence; not a claim of dramatic model gain.",
    ])

summary_lines.extend([
    "",
    "Limitation note:",
    "- Thermal values are relative intensity indicators (not direct Celsius).",
    "- Thermal (2012) and canopy (2021) datasets are from different years; interpretation is exploratory, not causal.",
])

(output_dir / "final_hotspot_summary.txt").write_text("\n".join(summary_lines), encoding="utf-8")

print("Evidence export completed.")
for fp in [
    output_dir / "hotspot_priority_cells.csv",
    output_dir / "hotspot_sensitivity_summary.csv",
    output_dir / "cluster_profile_summary.csv",
    output_dir / "model_comparison_summary.csv",
    output_dir / "final_hotspot_summary.txt",
]:
    print(f"- {fp}")

if export_warnings:
    print("Warnings:")
    for w in export_warnings:
        print(f"- {w}")

47. Final Notebook Quality Check¶

This final section runs a PASS/FAIL checklist over required columns, summaries, and export files. It acts as a final testing gate before submission and handover. The check helps confirm the notebook is complete and consistent for review.

# Compact PASS/FAIL checklist for Sprint 5 final testing.
from pathlib import Path

def check_item(condition, message):
    status = "PASS" if condition else "FAIL"
    print(f"{status} - {message}")
    return bool(condition)

checks = []
has_grid = "grid_gdf" in globals()
checks.append(check_item(has_grid and len(grid_gdf) > 0, "analysis grid exists"))

crs_alignment_ok = False
if "canopy_projected" in globals() and "thermal_src" in globals():
    try:
        crs_alignment_ok = (canopy_projected.crs == thermal_src.crs)
        if not crs_alignment_ok:
            crs_alignment_ok = (str(canopy_projected.crs) == str(thermal_src.crs))
    except Exception:
        crs_alignment_ok = False
checks.append(check_item(crs_alignment_ok, "CRS alignment evidence exists"))

checks.append(check_item(has_grid and "mean_thermal" in grid_gdf.columns, "mean_thermal column exists"))
checks.append(check_item(has_grid and "canopy_cover_pct" in grid_gdf.columns, "canopy_cover_pct column exists"))
checks.append(check_item(has_grid and "priority_cell" in grid_gdf.columns, "priority_cell column exists"))
checks.append(check_item(has_grid and "cluster_baseline" in grid_gdf.columns, "baseline cluster column exists"))
checks.append(check_item(has_grid and (("cluster_improved" in grid_gdf.columns) or ("cluster" in grid_gdf.columns)), "selected/improved cluster column exists"))
checks.append(check_item(("hotspot_sensitivity_summary_df" in globals()) or ("threshold_tuning_df" in globals()) or ("sensitivity_df" in globals()), "sensitivity/threshold summary exists"))
checks.append(check_item(("model_comparison_summary_df" in globals()) or ("comparison_table" in globals()), "model comparison summary exists"))
checks.append(check_item(has_grid and "hotspot_score_v2" in grid_gdf.columns, "hotspot_score_v2 exists"))

output_dir = Path("outputs")
expected_outputs = [
    output_dir / "hotspot_priority_cells.csv",
    output_dir / "hotspot_sensitivity_summary.csv",
    output_dir / "cluster_profile_summary.csv",
    output_dir / "model_comparison_summary.csv",
    output_dir / "final_hotspot_summary.txt",
]
for fp in expected_outputs:
    checks.append(check_item(fp.exists(), f"output file exists: {fp}"))

overall = all(checks)
print("\nOverall Sprint 5 QA status:", "PASS" if overall else "FAIL")
